prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and trade reshape labour demand, wages and the adjustment of local labour markets

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B027 with Autor, Hanson and Katz. I reassessed it against the chair's questions, and it holds on the common criteria. The question is first-order: who gains and loses when technology and trade shift labour demand, and how slowly and unevenly adjustment happens across skill groups and places. The evidence is cumulative. The skill-supply-and-demand work (Katz-Murphy, the education-versus-technology race), the task and polarisation evidence, and the local import-competition designs all rely on new data, transparent identification and an explanatory frame. As an economic historian I weight work that builds the empirical base and then tests it against alternatives, and this literature has done that for more than a decade. The core findings have survived replication and critique, and critiques have mainly refined magnitude, persistence and heterogeneity. On the chair's question about Katz, I would state his distinct, citable contribution as the long-run evidence that wage structure reflects the race between skill supply and technology-driven demand, plus the polarisation work with Autor. That is separate from his role in the mobility work on B028 and from the task-model theory, where Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane have claims outside this list. The citation should therefore name findings on labour demand, wages and adjustment, and not claim the task model as a discovery. On overlap with the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes, I think the marginal case holds. Those prizes concerned other questions: natural experiments in labour markets, women's labour-market outcomes, and institutions and prosperity. None established the joint evidence on how technology and trade shocks redistribute labour demand across workers and regions. If the committee cannot agree on a joint citation, I would accept Autor, Dorn and Hanson with a citation limited to import competition and local adjustment. I would accept Autor and Hanson as a last fallback, but I prefer the three-name joint version, because it credits both strands that the citation names.
statement.case_against: Attribution is still the main weakness. The three-name cap leaves out Dorn, a central co-author of the China-shock papers, and Katz's strand is partly separate from the import-competition work. The committee could reasonably read this as two prize-sized achievements joined by Autor. The task framework has contributors outside the credited names, including Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane. The size, persistence and external validity of the China-shock effects remain debated, and the designs identify local effects, so aggregate welfare claims need more structure than the evidence alone supplies. The citation I propose avoids effect sizes and aggregate claims, but that wording does not remove the underlying attribution cost. I also put this candidate first only after moving from my opening position. I opened with B017 first and B027 fourth, so I should be explicit that I moved on the substance of the maturity, breadth and citation-clarity arguments, not on the nine-file agreement.

responses.point: Friberg's round-1 file moved from Autor, Dorn and Hanson to Autor, Hanson and Katz. He argues the credited work should match the citation, that Katz anchors the skills and technology strand, and that a trade-shock-only trio would credit half of the achievement. He also treats the citation wording as the way to limit overlap with the Acemoglu task work.
responses.response: I note that my round-1 reply described your position as it was in the opening, and your file now names the same trio as mine. We agree on the main reasoning, which is that the credited names should match what the citation says. I am also persuaded by your wording point, so I keep the citation on labour demand, wages and local adjustment and do not cite the task model. Where I go further is on fallbacks. If the committee insists on a narrower citation, I would not defend Autor, Hanson and Katz under trade-shock wording. I would switch to Autor, Dorn and Hanson, because Dorn's claim on the import-competition papers is then stronger than Katz's. I think that is a choice about scope, not a disagreement over merit.

responses.point: Teorell raises the two-prizes concern: the task and skill-premium strand and the trade-shock strand may be separate achievements, and the Katz-Murphy lineage and the uncredited Levy and Murnane complicate credit. He says he would support Autor, Dorn and Hanson if the committee narrows the citation to trade exposure.
responses.response: I agree this is the main risk to a single citation, and your point that Dorn's claim on the trade-shock papers is at least as strong as Hanson's co-origination claim is fair. What I take from it is that the committee has to decide the scope of the citation before it decides the third name. The two strands share one empirical object: wage and employment responses of skill groups and local labour markets to shifts in labour demand. That is why I think a joint citation is coherent. The Katz-Murphy lineage argues for crediting him on supply-and-demand evidence on skills, not on task theory. I also share your caution about treating nine-file agreement as evidence of merit. For that reason I applied the common test again: could I write the citation without claiming more than the credited names produced?

responses.point: Hassler prefers B006 with Kiyotaki and Moore alone. He argues that attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist, that the mechanism is nearly thirty years old, and that it is distinct from the 2022 bank-focused prize. He says B027 needs a citation that holds across tasks, skill demand and trade shocks.
responses.response: Your attribution point is a real advantage over B027, and I take it seriously: a Kiyotaki-Moore award has no Dorn-type exclusion. I did not rank B006 in my opening, so I am relying on colleagues' descriptions here and have not independently verified them. Those descriptions suggest a mature, cleanly credited mechanism, and your argument that it works through asset prices and not through bank runs seems to me a credible answer to the redundancy worry. That moves B006 into my alternatives in place of B001. I still place B027 first because its main claims have been tested more directly against micro data in many settings, whereas the theory's quantitative importance is established more indirectly. My answer to your question about whether weaker identification is disqualifying is no. It is a reason to rank B006 below B027 on confirmation. It does not outweigh the attribution advantage if B027's citation cannot be agreed.

responses.point: Krusell's round-1 file moved from Autor and Hanson to Autor, Hanson and Katz. He argues the common question is how technology and trade shift labour demand and where adjustment lands, that Autor links the strands, and that the magnitude critiques refine persistence and concentration. He also rejects B017 on the grounds that measured misallocation may reflect measurement error and frictions.
responses.response: My round-1 reply addressed your two-name opening proposal, which your file no longer holds, so I now treat us as agreeing on the trio. On B017, I stay with my round-1 position that the measurement debate lowers its rank for me. Your point about the parallel Restuccia-Rogerson contribution also makes a clean citation harder to write. I have not reopened B017. On B012, you have argued that precursor work by Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and the proximity to the 2008 trade prize, complicate the credit. I take that seriously, but I still regard Helpman and Melitz as a mature two-person award with a clean originator claim for Melitz. That is why B012 is now my first alternative if B027 cannot be given a coherent citation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the technology and trade strands as one achievement or two, which determines whether Katz or Dorn is the better third name.
How far later critiques of China-shock magnitude, persistence and external validity weaken half of the citation, and whether a wording that avoids effect sizes is enough.
How much of the task-framework credit belongs to Acemoglu, Levy, Murnane and others outside the credited names, and what increment remains for Autor and Katz.
Whether B012 and B006, my fallbacks, are as clean as colleagues describe. I have not independently verified any source, and B006 was outside my opening ranking.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn, or for my alternatives B012 and B006. My co-authors and ties (Lund economic history, Lindvall, Cermeño, Schön, Kander and others) do not include a credited candidate. I have a general affinity for new-data and archival work and an interest in technological change, and I have tried to apply the same criteria across fields. I am a Lund colleague of committee member Tommy Andersson, which I disclose and do not treat as bearing on any candidate. This is disclosed, not adjudicated.
